articles.title: A Louisiana couple paid $429,000 for a home in 2021, then alleged a rotted underground air pipe, dead rodents in the ducts and other concealed defects; an appeals court has restored their case against the property brokerage for further hearings
articles.summary: A Louisiana couple who paid $429,000 for a house discovered a series of alleged hidden defects after moving in, including a rotted underground air pipe,
articles.body: A Louisiana couple who paid $429,000 for a house discovered a series of alleged hidden defects after moving in, including a rotted underground air pipe, rodent remains inside the air-conditioning ducts and problems with the swimming pool. They accused the sellers and real estate professionals involved in the transaction of concealing important information about the property's condition and sought damages over what they described as a home that was unfit to live in.In a November 18, 2026, decision available on Justia, the Louisiana Second Circuit Court of Appeal reversed a summary judgment that had dismissed the couple's claims against Group One Realty LLC, doing business as Coldwell Banker Realty One. The court ruled that questions remained about whether the real estate agent who handled the transaction was an independent contractor or an employee of the brokerage, meaning the case could not be dismissed at this stage. It sent the matter back to the district court for further proceedings without deciding whether the brokerage was ultimately liable.Couple discovered alleged defects after purchasing the houseThe case involved Janet Louise Payne Glisson and William Bradley Glisson, who agreed to purchase a property at 126 Llanfair Drive in Ruston, Louisiana, from Edward Jay Ellington and Kathy Riser Ellington. The sellers had signed an exclusive right-to-sell agreement with Group One Realty on May 18, 2021, naming John Christopher Stephenson as their agent. Three days later, the Glissons signed an agreement to purchase the house for $429,000. Stephenson also represented the buyers in the transaction, acting in a dual-agency capacity.The sale was completed on July 22, 2021, and the couple moved into the property on August 7. Before closing, inspections of the house and swimming pool had identified several problems, some of which were reportedly corrected. However, the buyers alleged that they began discovering numerous additional defects after moving in. These included hidden damage to a shed, a crack in the carport's concrete, a leaking sink beneath a cabinet and an underground rotted return-air pipe disconnected from the heating and cooling system.According to their lawsuit, the pipe contained stagnant groundwater and was open to the interior of the house, allowing foul-smelling air, insects and reptiles to enter. They also alleged that the air-conditioning ducts contained dead rodents and rodent droppings, the swimming pool was not functional and the gas supply to the furnace had been disconnected.Lawsuit accused sellers and real estate professionals of concealmentOn August 5, 2022, the Glissons filed a lawsuit seeking damages under Louisiana's redhibition law, along with claims involving breach of contract and fraud. They alleged that the defendants had knowingly misrepresented the property's condition and concealed significant defects before the sale. Group One challenged the claims, arguing that the buyers had waived their rights to seek redhibition damages, that the claims had prescribed and that the allegations against the brokerage were insufficiently specific.The district court initially dismissed the redhibition claims against Group One. The brokerage later sought summary judgment, arguing that Stephenson was an independent contractor rather than an employee and that it could not be held responsible for his alleged misrepresentations. The district court agreed, finding that the buyers had not established that Stephenson was an employee or that anyone associated with Group One knew about the alleged defects. It consequently dismissed the claims against the brokerage with prejudice.Appeals court found a factual dispute over the agent's statusThe Glissons challenged the decision, arguing that the brokerage's relationship with Stephenson required a closer examination before the claims could be dismissed. The appeals court explained that Louisiana law generally treats a sponsored real estate licensee as an independent contractor when certain statutory conditions are satisfied, including a valid written agreement with the sponsoring broker. However, the court noted that the existence of such an agreement does not automatically settle every question about the relationship.Group One had presented an independent agent agreement stating that Stephenson could determine his own working methods and that the brokerage had limited authority to direct his activities. However, the agreement also allowed either party to terminate their relationship at any time without specifying any liability for doing so.The appeals court considered this provision significant. It explained that whether someone is an employee or an independent contractor requires a fact-specific assessment, including the nature of the working relationship and the parties' rights and obligations. The judges concluded that reasonable people could disagree about whether the agreement's termination provision supported treating Stephenson as an employee for purposes of potential vicarious liability. That unresolved factual question made summary judgment inappropriate.Case returns to district courtThe Louisiana Second Circuit reversed the judgment dismissing the Glissons' claims against Group One Realty and remanded the matter for further proceedings. It also assessed the costs of the appeal against the brokerage. The ruling does not establish that the brokerage knew about the alleged defects or that it is liable for the couple's losses. Nor does it decide the underlying claims against the sellers or the agent's estate, which were not at issue in this appeal.Instead, the decision means the couple can continue pursuing their claims against the brokerage, with the disputed employment relationship requiring further consideration rather than being resolved through summary judgment.You use AI every day. articles.title: A UK shopkeeper who spent 42 years in Britain was told he had no right to live there after applying for a passport; at 76, Nelson Shardey has finally become a British citizen
articles.summary: For Nelson Shardey, Britain had been home for most of his adult life.
articles.body: For Nelson Shardey, Britain had been home for most of his adult life. He had arrived from Ghana as a student, worked in factories, built a business, raised two sons and became part of the community in Wallasey, Merseyside. Yet a passport application in 2019 brought an unexpected problem. Despite having spent more than four decades in the country, he was informed that he was not a British citizen and had no recognised right to remain. What followed was a lengthy immigration battle, a family-led campaign and renewed scrutiny of his circumstances by the Home Office. Now, at 76, the retired shopkeeper has finally received British citizenship.How Shardey went from a student from Ghana to a British shopkeeperShardey moved to the UK in 1977, travelling from Ghana to continue his education. Like many people who arrive in a new country, his early years involved taking whatever work was available. He found employment in the food industry, including at a Mother's Pride bread factory and businesses producing Kipling's Cakes and Bendicks chocolates.His working life eventually took him to Wallasey, where he settled and established a newsagent called Nelson's News. The shop became part of his life in the area, while his family ties grew through two marriages to British women. His second marriage resulted in two sons, Jacob and Aaron, who would later become closely involved in the campaign to resolve his immigration status.For decades, there had been little reason for him to question his position. He had worked, paid his way and lived openly in Britain. His right to remain had not been challenged by employers or authorities during his years of employment, according to his account.The 2019 passport request that turned his life upside downThe situation changed in 2019, when Shardey applied for a British passport so he could travel to Ghana following his mother's death. The application exposed a problem he had not anticipated: the authorities did not recognise him as a British citizen.He was informed that he would need to pursue a 10-year immigration route to settlement. The proposed process carried substantial costs, with an estimated £7,000 for the application route and a further £10,500 over the period to access NHS services. For a retired shopkeeper, finding that amount of money was far from straightforward.The decision also left him facing questions about his future in the country where he had spent much of his life. His circumstances had not changed, but the paperwork surrounding his status had become an obstacle to remaining there with certainty.How a family fundraising campaign helped change his immigration caseShardey's family refused to let the matter end with the initial response. His sons, Jacob and Aaron, helped organise a fundraising effort to support their father's legal case and bring attention to his circumstances. The campaign attracted backing from people across Wirral, with residents contributing to the effort to have the decision reconsidered.The renewed attention eventually led to the Home Office reviewing his case. Rather than requiring him to follow the standard immigration route, officials considered whether his circumstances justified an exception under the Immigration Act.The department ultimately accepted that discretion could be exercised outside the usual immigration rules. In 2024, Shardey was granted indefinite leave to remain, giving him permission to live in Britain without the restrictions attached to a temporary immigration status.That decision was a significant development, although it did not yet make him a British citizen. The family continued to hope that the recognition of his exceptional circumstances would lead to a more permanent resolution.At 76, he finally receives British citizenshipThe final step came in February 2026, when Shardey was granted full British citizenship. He attended a ceremony at Wallasey Town Hall, where the 76-year-old received his naturalisation certificate.Speaking afterwards, he described himself as extremely pleased with the outcome and expressed gratitude to the people who had supported the family throughout the process. He also spoke about his attachment to Britain, saying the experience had tested him and his relatives but had ultimately ended with a sense of belonging.For his sons, the response from the local community had been particularly striking. They described the support their father received as phenomenal, reflecting how widely the campaign had resonated with people in the area.A life in Wallasey recognised after years of uncertaintyShardey's connection with the community had extended beyond running his newsagent. In 2007, he received a police bravery award after intervening when a robber attacked a delivery worker with a baseball bat. He tackled the attacker, an incident that brought him recognition for his actions.After arriving in Britain in 1977, he had spent 42 years in the country by the time his passport application was rejected. Seven years after that setback, his citizenship has finally been confirmed. At an age when many people are long settled into retirement, Shardey has received formal recognition of the country he has called home for nearly five decades.You use AI every day. articles.body: While millions of players are still exploring the world of GTA 6, two streamers have already reached the finish line. One used an early time-zone advantage to claim the first completion, while the other turned his playthrough into a marathon that lasted more than two days. Their achievements have sparked excitement, but the rush to finish has also raised questions about experiencing a game built around its story.BrycexD becomes the first streamer to finish GTA 6 in under 40 hoursBrycexD secured the first reported streamer completion after finishing GTA 6 in 39 hours and 38 minutes. His broadcast also attracted significant attention, with the creator claiming that his viewership peaked at 14,000 across the platforms carrying his stream.His location played an important role in the race. That gave him valuable extra time to explore the story before many other players could even begin.The achievement came at a physical cost, though. articles.title: A Louisiana farmer returned from offshore work to find neighbours clearing trees from an 18-foot strip they believed was theirs; 13 years later, an appeals court upheld his land rights and awarded $59,966.99
articles.summary: A Louisiana farmer returned from offshore work in March 2013 to find neighbours clearing trees and brush from a strip of land he believed belonged to him.
articles.body: A Louisiana farmer returned from offshore work in March 2013 to find neighbours clearing trees and brush from a strip of land he believed belonged to him. The neighbours thought the land was part of their property because an old fence marked what they considered their boundary.The disagreement eventually turned into a 13-year legal battle. Now, the Louisiana Court of Appeal has upheld the farmer's ownership of the disputed land and ordered his neighbours to pay $59,966.99 for the damage caused by the clearing and changes to the property's drainage, according to Law Justia.The ruling was delivered on November 18, 2026, in the case of Benjamin Lee Bird v. William Eric Gill and Rhonda Marie Olivo Gill. According to the court's judgment, the dispute involved an 18-foot-wide strip measuring about 0.879 acres in Franklin Parish, Louisiana.An old fence led to a boundary disputeAccording to Law Justia, Benjamin Lee Bird bought his 114-acre property in 2004. His neighbours, William Eric Gill and Rhonda Marie Olivo Gill, bought an adjoining 100-acre property in March 2013.An old fence had been installed along the southern part of Bird's land sometime between 1988 and 1990. However, it did not follow the actual surveyed property boundary. An 18-foot strip between the fence and the Gills' legally established northern boundary therefore became the centre of the dispute.Before buying their property, William Gill inspected it with a farmer, David Fortenberry, to see whether it could be used for growing row crops. The previous owner told him that everything inside the fence belonged to the property.The Gills did not get a survey when they purchased the land. After the sale, William hired Fortenberry to prepare the property for farming and instructed him to work inside the fence. Fortenberry and another worker, Carey Williamson, began clearing trees and carrying out drainage work. When Bird returned from offshore work, he found that they were also working on the disputed strip.Bird told Williamson that he claimed ownership of approximately 20 feet of land beyond the fence. William Gill arrived, and the two men argued about where the boundary lay. Bird claimed that Gill said, “Let him waste his money on an attorney. I own it.” The court noted that there were no witnesses to this conversation.Clearing continued despite the disagreementWilliam Gill later spoke to his lawyer about the boundary. He said he understood from that conversation that the old fence might establish ownership. However, the lawyer testified that he did not remember the discussion and would not have advised anyone about ownership without qualifications. The court noted that neither side obtained a survey before the clearing work resumed.The workers removed and burned the trees and brush from the disputed strip. They also dug a new ditch across the land and used the removed soil to fill an existing ditch and other holes on the Gills' property. The Gills then levelled their land and created a slope that directed water north towards Bird's property. Bird said the changes increased flooding on his land.He filed a lawsuit on August 27, 2013, claiming ownership of the strip and accusing the neighbours of trespassing, removing trees and damaging the land. The Gills disputed his claim and argued that they had acquired ownership through long-term possession.A long court battleThe case went through several stages. An initial judgment in 2018 recognised Bird's ownership and awarded him damages. However, the Gills obtained a new trial after the court accepted that their lawyers' staff had made an honest scheduling mistake.The second trial took place over four days between December 2020 and October 2021. The trial court issued its final judgment in January 2026, again recognising Bird's ownership and awarding him $81,746.99. The Gills appealed both the ownership decision and the amount of damages.In its November 18 ruling, the Louisiana Second Circuit Court of Appeal upheld the decision recognising Bird's ownership. It also agreed that the neighbours were responsible for the damage caused by the clearing and changes to the land.Why the compensation was reducedThe appeals court reviewed each part of the damages awarded by the lower court. It upheld $45,000 for dirt work and drainage repairs, finding that the evidence supported the cost of restoring the land. An expert had estimated that the work would require more than 5,000 cubic yards of soil, along with heavy machinery and labour.The court also upheld $10,000 for replacing the removed trees. It noted that the trees had been burned, making it difficult to establish their exact number and type. Bird had estimated that around 130 trees were removed, while the neighbours' witnesses suggested that the number was much lower.However, the judges reduced the compensation for lost shade. The lower court had awarded $13,920 for three sheds, but the appeals court said the value of the replacement trees already included the shade they would provide. It allowed Bird $4,640 to reimburse him for one shed he had actually built to provide shade for his cattle while the case was pending.The court also removed the $2,500 award for fence repairs because there was not enough evidence showing the fence's condition before and after the clearing work. It cancelled the $10,000 awarded for mental anguish as well.The judges said Bird had not provided sufficient evidence of actual psychological injury caused by the property damage. The final compensation was therefore reduced from $81,746.99 to $59,966.99. The amount includes $45,000 for drainage and dirt work, $10,000 for tree replacement, $4,640 for shade replacement and $326.99 for a water trough.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Texas family found 9 long-lost World War II battleship records and artefacts in their late father's storage unit; the FBI authenticated the collection and returned it to the ship's museum
articles.summary: Nine historical records and artefacts missing from a World War II battleship for decades have been recovered after a Texas family discovered them in a
articles.body: Nine historical records and artefacts missing from a World War II battleship for decades have been recovered after a Texas family discovered them in a storage unit belonging to their late father. The items, which include documents connected to the ship's wartime operations and equipment, were voluntarily handed over and authenticated by the FBI. According to the FBI Boston Division, the recovered material has since been returned to the USS Massachusetts, a decommissioned battleship preserved as a museum at Battleship Cove in Fall River, Massachusetts, restoring an important collection of naval history.Texas family helps recover nine missing USS Massachusetts artefactsThe recovery of the nine items followed an unexpected discovery by a family in Texas. As reported by the FBI Boston Division in its September 2026 announcement, the family found the historical material among their late father's belongings in a storage unit. Their father had worked on refurbishing the USS Massachusetts during the 1990s, providing a connection between the collection and the battleship.Rather than keeping or disposing of the material, the family voluntarily relinquished the artefacts, allowing them to be returned to their original home. NBC 10 News also reported that the FBI's Dallas office examined and authenticated the recovered objects before they were handed back to the museum.The discovery brought an end to a period of uncertainty surrounding objects believed to have been missing for approximately three decades.What did the FBI recover from the battleshipThe recovered collection contains several items that offer insight into how the USS Massachusetts operated during the Second World War. According to the FBI, one of the most significant discoveries was a folder labelled Plan of the Day for 1942. The documents inside provide information about the Navy's operational planning during the conflict, offering researchers an opportunity to examine the ship's daily activities and organisation.Another recovered object was a rusted metal crate bearing the label Missile Hazards Within. Although the container's appearance reflects the passage of time, its label provides a glimpse into the equipment and safety considerations associated with the battleship.The collection also includes a First Lieutenant's Damage Control Book. The FBI said the book contains detailed engineering and structural specifications required to keep the vessel afloat and ready for combat. Such records help explain the technical work involved in maintaining a warship during military operations.NBC 10 News reported that the collection also included a large toolbox, which museum officials believe could eventually be displayed aboard the vessel.How the missing historical collection was tracedThe recovery was not the result of a routine search through old military records. Instead, it began when museum volunteers noticed something unusual online.According to the FBI Boston Division, the investigation started after volunteers at Battleship Cove spotted several missing items featured in a social media post. They alerted the museum's curator, who contacted the Fall River Police Department.The police subsequently approached the FBI on behalf of the museum, leading to an investigation by the Bureau's Boston Division in 2025. NBC 10 News reported that the case was eventually referred to the FBI's Art Crime Team, which specialises in investigating the theft and recovery of cultural property.Investigators worked with the FBI's Dallas Field Office to locate and secure the objects in Texas. The recovered material was then examined to establish its authenticity and connection to the USS Massachusetts.Importance of these recovered records for Battleship CoveThe USS Massachusetts, affectionately known by its crew as Big Mamie, is now preserved at Battleship Cove, a maritime museum in Fall River, Massachusetts. The vessel is a decommissioned World War II battleship and remains an important part of the museum's naval collection.The return of the nine objects gives the institution access to material that had been absent for decades. Christopher Nardi, chief operating officer of Battleship Cove, said the recovered documents and artefacts provide another way to understand the vessel's history.He also explained that the recovered records help bring together different elements of the battleship's history. Each item contributes information that can help researchers understand the vessel and the people who operated it.The artefacts will be preserved for future generationsThe return of the collection does not mean every object will immediately go on public display. According to NBC 10 News, museum officials are considering displaying some of the recovered items aboard the USS Massachusetts, including the large toolbox.More delicate documents will instead be protected and made available for research. This approach allows the museum to preserve fragile historical records while ensuring that researchers can still access their contents.The FBI's Art Crime Team has recovered more than 20,000 items valued at over $1 billion since its establishment, according to the agency's announcement.You use AI every day. articles.title: Customers buying washing machines, dishwashers and cookers from a UK retailer were automatically charged for optional recycling services; watchdog ordered refunds for nearly 40,000 shoppers and imposed a £720,000 fine
articles.summary: Marks Electrical has been fined £720,000 and ordered to refund nearly 40,000 customers after automatically charging them for optional recycling services
articles.body: Marks Electrical has been fined £720,000 and ordered to refund nearly 40,000 customers after automatically charging them for optional recycling services when they bought washing machines, dishwashers and cookers online. The Competition and Markets Authority ordered around £600,000 to be repaid, an average of £15 per customer, which takes the combined financial penalty to £1.32 million. The regulator announced its decision on 18 June 2026, and it was the second penalty imposed for a substantive breach of consumer law under its strengthened powers. The company admitted breaking the law and settled early, which cut its penalty by 40 per cent.Two recycling add-ons that Marks Electrical automatically opted customers into when they orderedAccording to GOV.UK, the Competition and Markets Authority found that the retailer pre-selected and charged customers for extra services without their express agreement. Customers who bought essential household items through the Marks Electrical website were opted into one or both of two services. The first, called Recycle Old Appliance, removed the customer’s old appliance at delivery so that it could be recycled. The second, called Unwrap and Recycle Packaging, unwrapped and removed the packaging of the new purchase at delivery for recycling.Why pre-ticked boxes for paid extras are illegal under consumer law, and which powered the regulator usedThe regulator said consumers must have a genuine choice over whether to pay for an optional extra, and that businesses are not allowed to use pre-ticked boxes or other forms of automatic opt-in for extras that cost money. Opting customers into additional payments without express consent is prohibited by the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, and the regulator used its powers under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 to impose the penalty. TLT noted that each service was added to the purchase through a pre-ticked box, so shoppers had to remove it actively before paying. The law firm also said the underlying rules are not new, but the regulator now has far tougher powers to fine breaches of them. Businesses that infringe consumer protection law can be fined up to 10 per cent of their global turnover, or £300,000 where that is higher.How long the pre-ticked charges ran and why the practice stoppedThe investigation looked at conduct from April 2025, when the regulator’s strengthened consumer powers came into force, to November 2025. GOV.UK reported that Marks Electrical stopped the conduct immediately after the investigation opened and engaged constructively with the regulator. By June 2026, the regulator said it had secured more than £1.3 million in refunds for customers and imposed fines totalling nearly £5 million under the same powers.How customers were refunded automatically and what the regulator said other businesses must doAffected customers did not need to take any action. Marks Electrical has managed the refunds, which went back to the payment method used for the appliance, or arrived by cheque if that was not possible, and customers were told by letter or email. Some refunds had already been paid when the penalty was announced, and each amount depends on how much the customer paid for the extras. Emma Cochrane, Executive Director of Consumer Protection at the Competition and Markets Authority, said in the announcement that people should be able to decide whether they want optional extras instead of being landed with costs they did not agree to, and that businesses should check their policies on automatic opt-ins because they should not be used. TLT advised retailers to make sure extras such as delivery upgrades, insurance, charity donations or gift wrapping are genuinely optional and never pre-selected, adding that charges a customer did not expressly agree to are void and can be refunded.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russian missiles, drone crash in Poland: Warsaw flags 'provocation' as Ukraine faces aerial barrage
articles.summary: Two Russian cruise missiles and a suspected jet-powered drone crashed in south-eastern Poland on Friday during a massive Russian aerial assault on Ukraine.
articles.body: Two Russian cruise missiles and a suspected jet-powered drone crashed in south-eastern Poland on Friday during a massive Russian aerial assault on Ukraine. The incidents prompted Warsaw to accuse Moscow of a possible “intentional provocation” and raised fresh concerns over the security of Nato territory.Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said the incidents appeared to be deliberate, noting that they coincided with major European military exercises in the country. The drills, which began on November 9, involve allied forces preparing for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.“We are dealing with an intentional provocation,” Tusk said.One of the Russian missiles is believed to have crashed around 35 kilometres from the area where the military exercises were under way. A Kh-101 cruise missile came down approximately 50 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, while the suspected jet-powered drone crashed around 30 kilometres from the border. There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage in Poland.There was no immediate response from Moscow.Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte described the incident as a “grave violation” of Polish airspace, linking it to Russia's ongoing military campaign against Ukraine.“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte wrote on X. He is expected to visit Poland over the weekend following the developments.The incident has renewed attention on Nato's collective security framework under Article 5, which treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all 32 members. However, the provision is not triggered automatically and requires a political decision by the alliance. Poland could also invoke Article 4, which provides for emergency consultations among member states.European leaders condemned the developments. British prime minister Andy Burnham called them “utterly unacceptable”, while European Council President António Costa said Russia “continues to spread (its) threats”. Germany's Foreign Ministry described the incident as “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.The crashes occurred during one of Russia's largest overnight attacks on Ukraine since its full-scale invasion in 2022. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had launched more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some carrying cluster warheads.At least eight people were killed and nearly 30 injured, according to Zelenskyy. Residential buildings, medical facilities, warehouses and bridges were also hit.Ukraine's deputy energy minister Artem Nekrasov said strikes on power infrastructure forced the country's three operational nuclear power plants to reduce generation, triggering emergency power cuts across 11 regions.Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to end the war remain uncertain. US president Donald Trump's envoys have discussed possible post-war security guarantees for Ukraine with European leaders. However, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov reiterated that even quasi-membership of Ukraine in Nato would be unacceptable to Moscow.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Georgia investor put nearly $2 million into three restaurants after being promised ownership stakes, but received none; appeals court upholds $650,000 fraud award and $525,025 in legal fees
articles.summary: A Georgia investor who put nearly $2 million into three restaurants after being promised a one-third ownership stake never received the interests he had
articles.body: A Georgia investor who put nearly $2 million into three restaurants after being promised a one-third ownership stake never received the interests he had been offered. Dr Naresh Parikh had also provided $145,000 in loans to Chittranjan Thakkar, who managed Green Chillies LLC, but the money was not repaid. Following a jury trial, Parikh was awarded $650,000 for fraud and $525,025.36 in attorney fees, in addition to the unpaid loans. On June 5, 2025, the Georgia Court of Appeals upheld the fraud and legal fee awards, finding sufficient evidence that Thakkar had made promises he did not intend to fulfil.Investor put nearly $2 million into three Georgia restaurants after being promised ownershipThe dispute involved three restaurants that were Gyro City in Hiram, Gyro City in Roswell and Santorini Taverna. According to the Georgia Court of Appeals' June 2025 ruling in Thakkar et al. v. Parikh, Dr Naresh Parikh had developed a friendship and business relationship with Chittranjan Thakkar before they discussed the restaurant investments.Parikh’s testimony revealed that Thakkar had told him he would get a third ownership in the restaurants for his investments in them. Parikh’s investments in the restaurants consisted of three promissory notes totalling $145,000 as well as another $2 million in investments for expenses related to running the restaurants. Even after the investments, Parikh received nothing in terms of ownership and was not repaid any of the money he loaned through those promissory notes.Also included were emails where Thakkar talked about how the ownership of the restaurants could be corrected to include Parikh. In court, Thakkar admitted that he could have arranged for some ownership changes but did not. The court observed that some of the money invested by Parikh in restaurant expenses was withdrawn and used for another business owned by Thakkar. These facts confirmed the jury’s decision that Parikh had been defrauded into investing, according to the Georgia Court of Appeals.Georgia appeals court upholds $650,000 fraud award but overturns $65 million punitive damagesFollowing the jury trial, Parikh received $650,000 jointly from Thakkar and Green Chillies LLC for fraud, along with $525,025.36 in attorney fees. Thakkar was also held responsible for repaying the separate $145,000 in promissory notes. The jury had additionally awarded $65 million in punitive damages.Thakkar and the company challenged the verdict, arguing that there was insufficient evidence to establish fraud and that the punitive damages were excessive. On June 5, 2025, the Georgia Court of Appeals upheld the fraud finding, the promissory note award and the attorney fees. It concluded that the evidence supported the jury's decision that Thakkar had promised ownership interests but failed to transfer them despite having the ability to do so.The court reached a different conclusion about the $65 million punitive damages award. It found the amount grossly excessive under the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, noting that the harm was economic, affected one individual and had already been addressed through compensatory damages. The judges therefore vacated the punitive award and sent that issue back for further proceedings. The $650,000 fraud compensation and more than $525,000 in attorney fees remained intact, as detailed in the court's published decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: US president Donald Trump on Friday defended his description of Russian president Vladimir Putin as a “friend”, but sidestepped a question on whether he considered the Russian leader a friend of the United States. Trump also maintained that Putin wanted to end the war in Ukraine, despite Moscow's continued attacks and its rejection of recent claims of progress in peace negotiations.“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said when asked whether Putin was a friend to the US, before shifting attention to his personal ties with the Russian president.“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with),” Trump said. “It’s actually very good.”The remarks came during a White House news conference following Trump's trip to China, where he held bilateral and trilateral meetings with Putin and Chinese president Xi Jinping. Trump had drawn attention during the visit for his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his “friend”.Reiterating his position on the Ukraine conflict, Trump said Putin wanted a diplomatic settlement, while suggesting that both Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy were struggling to end the fighting.“He’d love to end the war,” Trump said of Putin. “But you have two guys that don’t know how to end it. We’re trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelenskyy and Putin. They don’t know how to end it. They want to end it. They’re both stuck in it.”Trump's comments came hours after Russia launched a major overnight assault on Ukraine, killing at least eight civilians and injuring nearly 30, according to Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian president said Moscow had fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some carrying cluster warheads.Russia's attack followed Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. Russian President Putin had vowed retaliation for the damage to the strategically important bridge.The escalation also coincided with reports of two Russian missiles and a suspected drone crashing in Poland, prompting Warsaw to flag a possible Russian provocation.On the diplomatic front, US envoy Jared Kushner had said he believed Moscow was “comfortable” with Nato-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine. However, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov rejected the suggestion, saying even “quasi-membership” of Ukraine in Nato would be unacceptable.Asked about Russia's objections, Trump said negotiations should not be discussed publicly.“It is also a public relations war. And we’ll say things and they’ll say things,” he said, adding that he did not want to discuss security guarantees “because we got to get a deal first”.US secretary of state Marco Rubio defended Trump's engagement with world leaders, arguing that personal relationships between heads of state were important to diplomacy.“I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable,” Rubio said. “It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘If you target Americans, justice will find you’: FBI chief Kash Patel warns cyber criminals amid JPMorgan data breach, tech outages
articles.summary: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel on Friday (local time) warned cyber criminals targeting Americans that they would face justice,
articles.body: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel on Friday (local time) warned cyber criminals targeting Americans that they would face justice, saying the agency was stepping up its offensive against cyber threats under US President Donald Trump's leadership.In a post on X, Patel said 'Operation Winter Shield' was aimed at strengthening America's cyber defences and protecting businesses, government systems and critical infrastructure through cooperation with international partners.“Under President Trump’s leadership, this FBI is taking the fight to cyber criminals around the world,” Patel wrote.“Through Operation Winter Shield, we’re going on offence against cyber threats, strengthening our nation’s defences, and working with our partners to protect American businesses, government systems, and critical infrastructure,” he added.“Our message is simple: If you target the American people, justice will find you,” Patel said.His warning comes amid growing concerns over cybersecurity and digital infrastructure resilience in the US, following a cyberattack targeting third-party service providers associated with JPMorgan Chase that may have exposed personal information belonging to around 16,000 customers.JPMorgan Chase disclosed the incident on Thursday, saying its investigation indicated that attackers had accessed marketing data held by external vendors. The bank clarified that its core operations and services remained unaffected.“We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack. Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the bank said in its statement.According to Fox News, a ransomware group identified as n0n claimed responsibility for leaking the customer records. The incident also reportedly affected business partners associated with Visa and Mastercard, with the exposed information including email addresses, phone numbers and account IDs.The leaked information was reportedly linked to JPMorgan Chase's Reserve programme, an invitation-only Visa credit card generally requiring customers to have more than USD 10 million in assets under management.Reassuring customers, the bank said the breach was unrelated to a separate service disruption experienced earlier in the week and that affected customers would be contacted directly.“There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. There is no connection to the service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” JPMorgan Chase added.Visa indicated that the breach originated with a vendor in the Asia-Pacific region. However, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard maintained that their core payment networks and card numbers had not been compromised.The incident has drawn attention to the growing threat posed by attacks targeting third-party service providers, which can expose customer information even when a financial institution's internal systems remain secure.US cybersecurity leadership reshufflePatel's warning also comes amid changes in the Trump administration's cybersecurity leadership. The White House on Thursday named Kirsten A. Davies as acting head of the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), succeeding Sean Cairncross.Davies will hold the position in an acting capacity as the permanent appointment requires confirmation by the US Senate. Cairncross had overseen federal cybersecurity policy and strategy since August 2025.In a statement issued on Thursday night, Cairncross described his tenure as an "honour of a lifetime to serve" under President Trump.Following her appointment, Davies thanked Trump and senior administration officials in a post on X, outlining her vision for securing America's digital infrastructure.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also welcomed the appointment.“Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies. Look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity,” Rubio wrote.Series of technology disruptions raise concernsThe cyberattack comes during a turbulent period for America's financial and technology sectors, with several disruptions affecting businesses, government systems and essential services in recent weeks.Over the past few days, a software bug caused transaction-processing difficulties at JPMorgan Chase and several other banks. The disruption prompted the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to seek information to assess its impact and review customer communications, according to an industry executive.The financial sector's difficulties follow several high-profile technology disruptions, including a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that affected air travel last week, a global email outage at Microsoft and a major cyberattack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month.Recent reports have also pointed to malware being inserted into around 180 major websites, adding to concerns over the security of digital platforms.While official statements have largely ruled out cyberattacks as the cause of most of the recent non-financial outages, the incidents have intensified scrutiny of the resilience of America's digital infrastructure and the administration's approach to cybersecurity. articles.title: India, France condemn Pahalgam, Red Fort terror attacks at counter-terror meet
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India and France have condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including crossborder terrorism and violent extremism, and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India and France have condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including crossborder terrorism and violent extremism, and agreed to strengthen cooperation to tackle terror financing, online radicalisation and emerging technological threats.The two countries reiterated their strong condemnation of the April 22, 2025, terrorist attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, and the November 2025 terror incident near the Red Fort in New Delhi during the 18th meeting of the India-France Joint Working Group (JWG) on Counter Terrorism held in New Delhi on November 20.According to a ministry of external affairs (MEA) press release, the meeting was co-chaired by Suhel Ajaz Khan, Additional Secretary (Counter Terrorism) in the MEA, and Olivier Caron, French Ambassador-at-Large and Special Envoy for Counter-Terrorism and Organised Crime.During the discussions, both sides exchanged views on the prevailing terror threat in their respective regions and at the global level, including challenges posed by state-sponsored and cross-border terrorism.The two delegations also discussed ways to tackle traditional and emerging security challenges, particularly the misuse of new technologies and financial technologies by terrorist groups.The Indian side briefed the French delegation on its comprehensive National Counter Terrorism Policy and Strategy, PRAHAAR.Both countries also explored ways to deepen bilateral cooperation in combating terrorism through information sharing, capacity-building, training and the exchange of experiences and best practices. They also discussed measures to counter terror financing and online radicalisation.The two sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in multilateral forums, including the United Nations, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and the No Money for Terror (NMFT) initiative.The meeting concluded with both sides agreeing to hold the 19th meeting of the Joint Working Group in France on a mutually convenient date.The discussions reaffirmed India and France's commitment to stepping up joint efforts to counter terrorism and address evolving security challenges.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Would love to see him back': Donald Trump pitches Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday said he would like to see Jensen Huang return as chief executive of Nvidia, describing the technology entrepreneur as
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday said he would like to see Jensen Huang return as chief executive of Nvidia, describing the technology entrepreneur as one of the world's most brilliant minds and urging the company to give him a second chance.Speaking at a White House press conference, Trump said Huang should apologise for his actions and be allowed to resume his role at the chipmaking giant.“I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back,” Trump said.“I think the company, if they were smart, they'd take that brilliant man, accept an apology, and let him go back to work,” he added.Trump said Huang had made mistakes but argued that his contribution to the technology industry and America's position in the global artificial intelligence race should not be overlooked.“He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Mr. Trump said at a White House press conference. “We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them.The president also praised Huang for transforming Nvidia into one of the world's leading semiconductor companies, saying his work had helped strengthen America's position against China in the race for artificial intelligence dominance.“We would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Trump said. “That’s a very important company to us.”His remarks came about a week after Huang reportedly resigned from Nvidia following allegations of affairs with a company executive and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.The allegations have also raised national security concerns in Washington, with lawmakers examining whether sensitive company information or advanced Nvidia chips could have been accessed or transferred to Chinese entities.Congressional committee chairmen are gathering information from Huang and Nvidia over potential security breaches. Lawmakers have expressed concerns that the alleged relationship involving Alice Huang could have exposed trade secrets or facilitated the transfer of advanced semiconductor technology to Chinese companies.Nvidia, meanwhile, has signalled that it is preparing for a leadership transition, with the company reportedly considering both internal and external candidates for the CEO position.Huang transformed Nvidia from a company primarily associated with gaming graphics processors into a major force in the global semiconductor industry. Its chips have become central to the development and deployment of artificial intelligence systems.Trump backs Commerce Secretary Howard LutnickTrump also defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against criticism over the administration's handling of export controls on Nvidia chips.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had suggested in media interviews that the Commerce Department was not sufficiently stringent in controlling access to the advanced semiconductors.Asked whether he had lost confidence in Lutnick, Trump rejected the suggestion that the secretary should be replaced.“I have not lost confidence [in Mr. Lutnick],” Trump said.“He’s a different kind of guy,” he said. “He’s a natural businessman.”You use AI every day. articles.title: An Illinois couple installed a fence after reporting trespassers near their bedroom window and a car theft, but their HOA challenged its placement; November 17 appeals judges upheld an order to move it
articles.summary: A fence that was meant to help a family feel safe in their own home has become the focus of a legal battle in an Illinois neighborhood, raising questions
articles.body: A fence that was meant to help a family feel safe in their own home has become the focus of a legal battle in an Illinois neighborhood, raising questions about the rights of homeowners and the power of homeowners associations. Vincent and Lekeisha Williams reported repeated trespassing, a stolen car and concerns for their family's security, and erected a fence around their property. But their neighborhood association challenged the placement of the structure, saying it violated community restrictions. The dispute eventually made its way to an appeals court, which has now upheld an earlier order that the couple move the fence.A couple built a fence for safetyThe Appellate Court of Illinois said the dispute involved the Williams family, who owned a home in the Ashford Farms subdivision in St. Clair County. The couple had had a number of security incidents involving people on their property and appearing near their bedroom window. Lekeisha Williams testified at trial that the family had called police on several occasions about their trespassing concerns. To make matters worse, their vehicle was stolen from the yard. Vincent Williams also shared stories about their business, including the burglaries at the family pharmacy.Fearing for their safety, the couple opted to put a fence that would surround areas around their house that were vulnerable, including windows and an electrical box. They said the structure had helped to avoid further incidents. But the fence’s location soon led to a dispute with the Ashford Farms Homeowners Association.HOA disputes placement of fence per community guidelinesThe Illinois Appellate Court said restrictive covenants in the subdivision required residents to obtain written architectural approval before putting up fences or making certain changes to the outside of their homes. The rules also restricted fencing in certain areas of residential properties and gave the association’s architectural committee authority over the placement, height and materials of approved structures. The committee initially rejected the Williamses’ preferred placement, but later proposed a compromise to allow the fence to extend to about the middle of their house. But the couple put it further forward in the home. They were issued a compliance notice in March 2023 and given 30 days to rectify the violation, but did not remove the structure. The association then sued to enforce the neighborhood restrictions.Court dismisses couple’s selective enforcement argumentIn October 2024, the Williamses argued at the bench trial other properties in the subdivision had fences that apparently violated similar requirements. They also provided evidence of the trespass incidents and explained that the alternate location suggested by the association would not provide sufficient protection to the area adjacent to their bedroom window. However, the association’s property manager testified that another homeowner with a fence in a similar situation was also sued and told to take it down.In April 2025, the trial court found in favor of the association, ruling that the couple had installed the structure without the required approval. It ordered them to move the fence back to the previously approved location within 120 days but denied the association attorney fees.Appeals court supports fence move orderThe Williamses appealed, saying their fence met the subdivision’s restrictions and that the association was picking and choosing which rules to enforce. They also questioned whether the architectural committee had properly approved the installation by failing to respond within the 60-day period required.But the Appellate Court of Illinois, Fifth District, denied their appeal and affirmed the lower court’s judgment in its November 17, 2026 decision.The judges decided the couple needed to get architectural approval even if the fence did not go all the way to the street. The committee had given permission for the structure to be installed halfway along the house but not at the front of the property. The court also found that not enough evidence of selective enforcement. The other homeowner the couple named had already gone through similar legal action and was told to take down a fence that had been put up illegally.As for the 60-day approval argument, the appeals judges refused to consider it because the couple had not raised the issue in the original trial. The court noted that the association was denied the opportunity to respond to the new argument raised at the stage of appeals.The ruling, issued on November 17, therefore upholds the original order to relocate the fence and requires the Williamses to move the fence to the position approved by the association.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: Would you share your data for public good?
articles.summary: When a website asks you to accept its cookies, odds are you do it without much thought.
articles.body: When a website asks you to accept its cookies, odds are you do it without much thought. What was meant to be a data privacy safeguard has become an empty ritual. But what if such privacy laws are counterproductive in ways that we have not considered? That’s the contrarian claim Omri Ben-Shahar, a University of Chicago law professor, makes in his book Why Fear Data.Ben-Shaharargues that these laws have misdiagnosed the problem. Yes, they shield individuals from intrusion, which is a private harm, but they pay little attention to the possible good that masses of data could deliver. Those gains, he says, would be enormous, measured in lives, injuries and dollars rather than convenience. He explains this with examples.Take roads first. Every year, more than 40,000 Americans die in road accidents, which is about a fourth of road deaths in India annually. Would drivers be more careful if they could save on insurance premiums? Experience shows they are. Where insurers offer opt-in policies that track how you drive – hard braking, sharp turns, phone use – and cut premiums for safe drivers, fatal accidents are around 30% lower among those who are tracked.In US, such policies can potentially save 12,000 lives a year. Only if you are willing to share your data with insurers. But Ben-Shaharsays state govts have created hurdles for such data sharing. California, for example, bans tracking anything beyond miles driven, and some states stop insurers from using texting data against drivers.Facial recognition is another intrusive tech that can do good, he argues. In US, a facial recognition tool is said to have helped identify over 18,000 trafficking victims. In India, another app called Darpan reportedly helped rescue over 3,000 missing children in a month-long operation in 2020.But you can’t use this tech in EU, where scraping faces off the internet is banned. Critics say such software is responsible for wrongful arrests of Black men, but that problem also arises from a paucity of training data. If privacy rules are relaxed, to train AI on better quality data, the mistakes will reduce.Ben-Shahar’sthird example is about health records. In Malawi, he says, digitising HIV patients’ files cut deaths by 28% within five years – preventing over 5,000 deaths. However, the HIV death rate could have fallen more had many patients not opted out of digitisation on privacy grounds.Denying access to patient data slows down research also. For example, consent for follow-up data analysis fell from 96% to 34% once America’s HIPAA rules demanded formal consent. By one estimate, an eight-month delay to a 1980s heart attack drug trial, caused by consent paperwork, cost some 9,000 lives.Ben-Shaharconsiders this a case of precaution run amok. Privacy, once valued as a means to a good life, has become an end in itself – he calls it privacy fundamentalism. To a large extent, fear of China’s surveillance state, rumoured to be hungry for everybody’s data, is used as a bogeyman for hermetic data privacy laws. He clarifies that he doesn’t consider privacyworthless, but urges everyone to weigh both sides of the ledger. Because a law that counts only the harms of data sharing will always say no.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Understanding Vs knowing: Looking beyond filters
articles.summary: By: Ganesh Kolambakar We often believe that we understand something simply because we know about it. But is knowing the same as understanding?
articles.body: By: Ganesh KolambakarWe often believe that we understand something simply because we know about it. But is knowing the same as understanding? And do we see things as they are, or merely as we perceive them? Understanding something is the ability to recognise relationships, connections and implications, and to apply what we know with clarity and discernment.But can we ever see reality exactly as it is? Our perceptions are shaped by our upbringing, experiences, beliefs, conditioning and emotions. What we consider truth may simply be our interpretation of it. We often mistake our perspective for reality and our assumptions for facts. Consequently, our understanding is influenced by the filters through which we view the world. Although we may never comprehend reality in its entirety, we can continually refine our understanding by becoming aware of these limitations.The Jain philosophy of Anekantavad offers a profound insight into this limitation. It recognises that reality has multiple dimensions and that no single perspective can capture it entirely. The familiar parable of the blind men and the elephant illustrates this beautifully. Each man touches a different part of the elephant and describes it according to his experience. One calls it a pillar, another a rope and yet another a fan. Each describes what he experiences, but none comprehends the whole elephant.Anekantavad does not suggest that every opinion is equally correct. Rather, it encourages us to remain receptive to other perspectives and avoid treating our partial knowledge as the complete truth. As we gain new experiences and insights, we must be willing to revisit and revise what we previously believed.Advait Vedanta offers another dimension to this exploration through the concepts of maya and avidya. Maya is associated with the appearance of multiplicity and the veiling of underlying reality, while avidya represents ignorance and misconceptions about our true nature. Together, these concepts help explain why we often mistake appearances for reality and identify ourselves with our thoughts, roles, emotions and possessions.This brings us to an important distinction between information, knowledge and understanding. Information gives us facts; knowledge helps us connect and organise those facts; understanding enables us to recognise their meaning, implications and relevance. Knowledge is having the pieces; understanding is seeing the picture they make. We know we have understood something when we can explain it simply, apply it in different situations, recognise its limitations and appreciate how a change in one element affects the whole.However, understanding cannot remain an intellectual exercise. It must find expression in everyday life. Consider a situation where someone becomes angry with us. Our immediate response may be to feel offended, defend ourselves or retaliate. But a deeper understanding allows us to recognise the other person’s anger without allowing it to determine our own emotional response. We can distinguish their emotion from our own and choose not to get drawn into it. This does not mean accepting inappropriate behaviour or avoiding necessary action. It means responding with awareness rather than reacting impulsively.Ultimately, understanding is a continuous process of looking beyond the filters through which we view ourselves and the world. It is about seeing more clearly, recognising what we may have missed and remaining open to new insights.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: ‘Will you marry me?’ Australian MP Jordan Lane proposes to long-time partner during farewell speech in Parliament
articles.summary: Valedictory speeches in Parliament usually stick to policy wins, political thank-yous, and career reflections. Jordan Lane had something else in mind.
articles.body: Valedictory speeches in Parliament usually stick to policy wins, political thank-yous, and career reflections. Jordan Lane had something else in mind.On Thursday, November 19, the 32-year-old Liberal Party MP for Ryde caught colleagues off guard in Sydney's New South Wales (NSW) Parliament by pulling out a ring and proposing to his partner of more than ten years, Natalie, right in the middle of his final address.Natalie was sitting in the public gallery of the Legislative Assembly as Lane wrapped up his time in state politics - and watched as he turned his closing remarks into a marriage proposal.Australian MP Jordan Lane pops the question in ParliamentNearing the end of his speech, Lane reached for an engagement ring and looked up toward Natalie.“Speaker, my final question as the member for Ryde is to my great love, Natalie. Will you marry me?” he asked.Lawmakers erupted into cheers and applause as Lane dropped to one knee. Natalie said yes, and the pair shared a kiss after he slipped the ring onto her finger.Ever the parliamentarian, Lane made sure the exchange went into the official record, quipping, “I would like to note for Hansard that she said ‘yes’.”The light-hearted moment drew grins from both sides of the chamber. NSW Legislative Assembly Speaker Greg Piper played along, remarking, “The 58th parliament will be recalled as the ‘parliament of love’.”Why is Jordan Lane stepping away from politics?The proposal arrived just days after Lane confirmed he will not seek re-election when NSW voters head to the polls in March 2027. While he has now delivered his farewell speech ahead of the parliamentary break, he isn't contesting the upcoming state election—joining a growing list of Liberal MPs who have announced plans to bow out before the March 2027 vote, according to The Guardian.During his valedictory remarks, Lane opened up about stepping back from public life, talking candidly about how love has steered his priorities and how tough it can be to put deeply personal choices into words on the floor of Parliament.From Ryde’s youngest mayor to state MPLong before entering state Parliament, Lane had already built a busy career in local government. Elected to the NSW Legislative Assembly on March 25, 2023, he also served on the City of Ryde Council from 2017 to 2024.Back in January 2022, at just 27 years old, he became the youngest mayor in Ryde’s history, according to the City of Ryde.Outside politics, Lane earned both bachelor’s and master’s degrees in commerce from the University of Sydney, and worked in disability advocacy and project management before moving into state office.His farewell speech may have closed the door on his run in Macquarie Street - but it kicked off a brand-new chapter with a wedding on the calendar.

articles.title: ‘Justice at last’: Rohingya refugees welcome UN court action against Myanmar
articles.summary: For hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar, a landmark ruling by UN court recognising Myanmar’s 2017 military crackdown as genocide has
articles.body: For hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar, a landmark ruling by UN court recognising Myanmar’s 2017 military crackdown as genocide has brought renewed hope for justice and a safe return home. Refugees gathered around a large screen at the camp on Thursday to follow the verdict, which many described as a “small victory”.The court held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya minority, marking the first time it has ruled that a state committed the crime. It also ordered Myanmar to ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees, pay reparations and prosecute those suspected of involvement in the atrocities.However, refugees told The Washington Post that the ruling was only the beginning of their fight. “Justice has started,” said Mohammad Rofik, a Rohingya community leader, adding that they still had “a long way to go”.The judgment comes nearly nine years after Myanmar’s military launched a clearance operation in Rakhine state in August 2017, following an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The crackdown was accompanied by allegations of mass killings, sexual violence and the burning of thousands of homes. The ICJ said evidence showed Myanmar's forces killed around 10,000 Rohingya.Despite the legally binding nature of the verdict, its implementation remains uncertain as the court has no independent enforcement mechanism. Myanmar's government on Friday dismissed the ruling as “unfair”.Around 1.2 million Rohingya refugees currently live in Bangladesh, most in overcrowded camps in Cox’s Bazar, facing poor sanitation, disease, fire hazards and restrictions on employment. articles.body: MUMBAI: A Nov 19 meeting chaired by revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule is likely to pave the way for transferring a 5,513-sq-metre fire station plot on Veera Desai Road, Andheri, to the state govt.On Friday, BJP corporator Rupesh Sawarkar met BMC commissioner Ashwini Bhide, seeking completion of the land transfer and construction tender process within 90 days. Sawarkar said the area urgently needed a fire station. In a letter to Bhide, he said private owners had handed over the plot at the Nov 19 meeting, but official communication was awaited.The demand follows the Nov 7 fire at Runwal Elegante, Lokhandwala, in which 46-year-old lift operator Dhanpat Mahatu died of smoke inhalation. While officials said fire tenders reached promptly, residents believe a local fire station would improve response times.The BMC's K-West ward demolished an unauthorised garage and marriage hall on the plot in September following residents' complaints.
